18.about: Chopin’s first published waltz, subtitled ’Grande valse brillante’, a bright, extroverted showpiece in the tradition of the Viennese ballroom waltz but elevated with Chopin’s characteristic elegance and virtuosic flourishes.
18.ctx: Composed in 1833 and published the following year, dedicated to Chopin’s pupil Laura Horsford, the piece established the model — a brilliant concert waltz rather than a functional dance piece — that Chopin’s later waltzes would follow.
facts: Chopin’s first published waltz.
Subtitled ’Grande valse brillante’.
Set the pattern of the brilliant concert waltz that Chopin’s later waltzes followed.

23.about: The first of Chopin’s four ballades and one of the towering works of the Romantic piano repertoire, a sweeping, narrative-like piece that moves from a brooding opening through several dramatic transformations to a stormy, virtuosic close. Chopin essentially invented the piano ballade as a genre, inspired by the narrative poetry of his fellow Pole Adam Mickiewicz.
23.ctx: Composed over several years between Vienna and Paris and published in 1836, dedicated to Baron Nathaniel von Stockhausen, the piece established the ballade as a large-scale, narrative single-movement genre for piano that Liszt, Brahms and others would later adopt.
facts: Chopin effectively invented the piano ballade as a musical genre.
Believed to have been inspired by the narrative poetry of Adam Mickiewicz.
One of the most frequently performed works in the entire piano repertoire.

31.about: The second and most popular of Chopin’s four scherzos, built on a dramatic contrast between a hushed, questioning opening gesture and sudden, explosive outbursts, framing a broad, lyrical central melody.
31.ctx: Composed in 1837 and dedicated to his pupil the Countess Adele Furstenstein, the scherzo shows Chopin, like Beethoven before him, transforming the scherzo from a lighthearted dance movement into a large-scale, dramatically serious concert genre.
facts: The most frequently performed of Chopin’s four scherzos.
Built on a famous opening contrast between a hushed question and a loud answer.
Part of Chopin’s transformation of the scherzo into a serious, large-scale genre.

35.about: Chopin’s best-known piano sonata, built around its third movement, the famous ’Funeral March’, composed separately two years before the rest of the sonata and later incorporated into it. The finale, a brief, eerie unison passage often described as ’wind over graves’, was considered so strange in its own time that even Schumann, an admirer of Chopin, professed himself bewildered by it.
35.ctx: Composed in stages between 1837 and 1839, with the famous Funeral March written first in 1837 and the surrounding movements added over the following two years, including during Chopin’s difficult winter in Majorca. The march became so famous independently of the sonata that it has been used at state funerals, including those of many prominent political and cultural figures, ever since.
parts: A restless, agitated scherzo with a lyrical trio.
The famous funeral march, composed two years before the rest of the sonata.
A brief, eerie movement of rushing unison notes, sometimes described as ’wind over graves’.
facts: Its third movement, the Funeral March, was composed two years before the rest of the sonata.
The march has been played at numerous state funerals since Chopin’s own death.
Schumann admitted he found the strange, sparse finale bewildering.

52.about: The last and most structurally sophisticated of Chopin’s four ballades, weaving its themes together with exceptional contrapuntal and harmonic subtlety before erupting into one of the most technically formidable codas in the piano repertoire.
52.ctx: Composed in 1842, during the summer Chopin spent at George Sand’s country estate at Nohant, and dedicated to Baroness Charlotte de Rothschild, the ballade is widely regarded by scholars and pianists as the summit of Chopin’s achievement in the genre.
facts: Widely considered the most structurally sophisticated of Chopin’s four ballades.
Composed at George Sand’s country estate, Nohant.
Ends with one of the most technically demanding codas in the piano repertoire.

53.about: Nicknamed the ’Heroic’ Polonaise, one of the most famous works in the entire piano literature, built on a grand, triumphant main theme and a central section built from thundering left-hand octaves said to evoke a cavalry charge, demanding exceptional stamina from the performer.
53.ctx: Composed in 1842 and dedicated to Auguste Leo, the polonaise represents the culmination of Chopin’s lifelong reinvention of the Polish national dance as a vehicle for large-scale, heroic musical statement, tinged with the patriotism of a composer permanently exiled from his homeland.
facts: Nicknamed the ’Heroic’ Polonaise.
Its central section, built from thundering octaves, is said to evoke an approaching cavalry charge.
One of the most popular and frequently performed works in the piano repertoire.

66.about: One of Chopin’s most beloved works, a swirling, restless outer section framing a broad, singing central melody; Chopin never published it and reportedly considered it unworthy of his other work, but it became immensely popular after being issued posthumously by his friend Julian Fontana against his wishes.
66.ctx: Composed around 1834 but withheld from publication by Chopin himself throughout his life, the piece was published in 1855, six years after his death, by Fontana, who had been entrusted with organizing Chopin’s unpublished manuscripts.
facts: Chopin never published it during his lifetime.
Published posthumously in 1855 by his friend Julian Fontana.
One of the most frequently performed of all Chopin’s works despite his own reservations about it.

9/2.about: The most famous of Chopin’s twenty-one nocturnes, a gently ornamented, songlike piece whose melody grows more elaborately decorated each time it returns — a hallmark of Chopin’s operatic, bel-canto-inspired approach to the nocturne, a genre he inherited from the Irish composer John Field.
9/2.ctx: Composed around 1830–31 and published in 1833 as part of the set of three nocturnes, Op. 9, dedicated to Marie Pleyel, the piece has become one of the most widely recognized pieces of piano music ever written, a fixture of both the concert repertoire and popular culture.
facts: The most famous of Chopin’s twenty-one nocturnes.
Chopin inherited the nocturne genre from the Irish composer John Field.
Its melody becomes more ornately decorated with each repetition.

27/2.about: Widely regarded as one of Chopin’s finest nocturnes, built on a long, arching melodic line over a gently rocking accompaniment, with a central section of increasingly ornate, improvisatory figuration before the opening melody returns transformed.
27/2.ctx: Composed in 1835 and published in 1837 as the second of the two nocturnes of Op. 27, dedicated to the Countess d’Appony, from a period when Chopin was consolidating his mature, highly personal style of piano writing.
facts: Often ranked among the finest of Chopin’s twenty-one nocturnes.
Dedicated to the Countess d’Appony.
Its melody returns in an increasingly ornamented form.

posth-cs.about: Marked ’Lento con gran espressione’, this nocturne was not published in Chopin’s lifetime and only appeared in print decades after his death, yet it has become one of his most performed short works, prized for its intimate, improvisatory melancholy. It gained further fame in the twenty-first century from its prominent use in the film The Pianist.
posth-cs.ctx: Composed around 1830, likely for Chopin’s sister Ludwika, before his permanent departure from Poland, the piece was kept privately within the family and only published in 1875, long after Chopin’s death, which is why it carries no opus number.
facts: Not published until 1875, decades after Chopin’s death.
Prominently featured in the 2002 film The Pianist.
Believed to have been written for his sister Ludwika.

10/3.about: Nicknamed ’Tristesse’ (Sadness) though not by Chopin himself, this étude is built almost entirely from a broad, singing melody rather than the technical figuration typical of the genre — Chopin reportedly said he had never written a more beautiful melody, and wept when a student played it back to him.
10/3.ctx: Composed in 1832 as part of the twelve études of Op. 10, dedicated to Franz Liszt and published in 1833. Unlike most of its companions, which drill a specific technical figure, this étude is prized above all for its melodic beauty.
facts: Chopin reportedly called its melody the most beautiful he ever wrote.
Its nickname, ’Tristesse’, was not given by Chopin.
The set of twelve études, Op. 10, is dedicated to Franz Liszt.

10/5.about: Nicknamed the ’Black Key’ étude because the right hand plays exclusively on the piano’s black keys throughout, a technical and coloristic experiment that produces a bright, pentatonic-flavoured sound world unusual for its time.
10/5.ctx: Composed around 1830, part of the twelve études of Op. 10 that established Chopin’s reputation as both a visionary pianist and a serious composer, transforming what had been a purely pedagogical genre into concert repertoire.
facts: The right hand plays exclusively on black keys.
Part of the Op. 10 études dedicated to Franz Liszt.
One of the most frequently performed of all Chopin’s études.

10/12.about: Nicknamed the ’Revolutionary’ étude, a stormy, turbulent piece built on relentless, driving left-hand figuration under a defiant right-hand melody. Legend links its composition to Chopin’s anguish on hearing that Warsaw had fallen to Russian forces during the 1830–31 uprising, though the story’s precise accuracy is debated by scholars.
10/12.ctx: Traditionally dated to 1831, when Chopin, then in Stuttgart, is said to have received news of the fall of Warsaw to Russian troops, ending the November Uprising. The nickname ’Revolutionary’ was attached long after the fact and was never used by Chopin himself, though the association has become inseparable from the piece.
facts: Nicknamed ’Revolutionary’, a title not given by Chopin.
Traditionally linked to his reaction to the fall of Warsaw in 1831.
Closes the set of twelve études, Op. 10.

25/9.about: Nicknamed the ’Butterfly’ étude for its light, fluttering right-hand figuration that leaps across wide intervals, brief and effervescent, offering a moment of relief amid the more technically demanding studies surrounding it in the Op. 25 set.
25/9.ctx: Composed in the mid-1830s as part of the second set of twelve études, Op. 25, dedicated to Liszt’s companion Marie d’Agoult and published in 1837.
facts: Nicknamed the ’Butterfly’ étude for its fluttering figuration.
One of the shortest and lightest of Chopin’s twenty-seven études.
Part of the Op. 25 set dedicated to Marie d’Agoult.

25/11.about: Nicknamed the ’Winter Wind’ étude, one of the most technically demanding pieces in the entire piano repertoire, pitting a simple, chorale-like melody in the left hand against a ferocious, unrelenting torrent of right-hand figuration.
25/11.ctx: Composed in 1836, near the end of work on the Op. 25 études, the piece represents the summit of technical difficulty within Chopin’s études, requiring extraordinary stamina and precision across its unbroken storm of notes.
facts: Nicknamed the ’Winter Wind’ étude.
Considered one of the most technically demanding of all Chopin’s études.
Near the end of the second set of études, Op. 25.

28/15.about: Nicknamed the ’Raindrop’ Prelude for its persistently repeated note, said to evoke rain falling on the roof of the monastery in Majorca where Chopin composed it while his health was failing. The outer sections are serene, but the central episode turns dark and funereal before the opening material returns.
28/15.ctx: Composed during the difficult winter of 1838–39 that Chopin spent in Majorca with the writer George Sand, part of the complete set of twenty-four preludes, Op. 28, covering every major and minor key and modeled on J. S. Bach’s Well-Tempered Clavier. Chopin was seriously ill with what was likely early tuberculosis during this stay.
facts: Nicknamed the ’Raindrop’ Prelude for its repeated note.
Composed while Chopin was seriously ill in Majorca.
Part of the complete set of twenty-four preludes, Op. 28, one in every key.

64/1.about: Nicknamed the ’Minute Waltz’, although Chopin never claimed it could actually be played in sixty seconds — the nickname, referring instead to its small (’minute’ in the sense of tiny) scale, was misread over time as a challenge about tempo. According to a popular but unverified story, it was inspired by watching George Sand’s small dog chase its own tail.
64/1.ctx: Composed in 1846–47, among the last works Chopin published in his lifetime, dedicated to the Countess Delfina Potocka, part of the three waltzes of Op. 64 published in 1847, two years before his death.
facts: Its nickname refers to its small scale, not literally to a sixty-second performance time.
Popularly, but unverifiably, associated with George Sand’s pet dog.
One of the last works Chopin published before his death.

34/2.about: A melancholy waltz in A minor, slower and more introspective than the brilliant salon waltzes surrounding it, built on a wistful, repeating melodic figure that gives the piece an unusually plaintive, songlike character for a dance form.
34/2.ctx: Composed over several years and published in 1838 as the second of the three ’Grandes valses brillantes’, Op. 34, dedicated to Chopin’s pupil Josephine Baroness d’Este.
facts: The second of the three waltzes of Op. 34.
Notably more melancholy in character than most of Chopin’s other waltzes.
Dedicated to his pupil, the Baroness d’Este.

9/1.about: A languid, bel-canto nocturne whose long, improvisatory right-hand melody drifts freely over a steady rocking bass, decorated with ever more elaborate roulades on each return, in the ornamented Italian-opera style Chopin absorbed from Bellini.
9/1.ctx: The first of the three Op. 9 nocturnes, composed around 1830–31 and dedicated, along with its companions, to Marie Pleyel, wife of the piano-maker Camille Pleyel. It set the template for Chopin’s lifelong reinvention of John Field’s nocturne genre.
facts: The first of the three Op. 9 nocturnes.
Dedicated, with the set, to Marie Pleyel.
Shows the influence of Italian bel canto opera.

9/3.about: A playful, capricious nocturne in B major whose sunny outer sections frame an agitated, stormy middle section in B minor, a dramatic contrast unusual for the genre at the time.
9/3.ctx: The last of the three Op. 9 nocturnes, composed alongside its two companions around 1830–31 and published in 1833. Its brighter mood and turbulent centre point toward the more dramatic nocturnes Chopin would write later in the decade.
facts: The third of the three Op. 9 nocturnes.
Its stormy middle section is unusually turbulent for an early nocturne.
Composed around 1830–31, before Chopin settled permanently in Paris.

15/1.about: A serene, songful F major melody is twice interrupted by a stormy con fuoco outburst in F minor, before the opening calm returns to close the piece — an early instance of the sharply contrasted drama Chopin would use throughout the genre.
15/1.ctx: The first of the three Op. 15 nocturnes, composed in stages between 1830 and 1833 and dedicated to Chopin’s friend Ferdinand Hiller. Its abrupt mood-swing between reverie and turbulence was noted by contemporaries as a striking departure from Field’s gentler model.
facts: The first of the three Op. 15 nocturnes.
Dedicated to the composer Ferdinand Hiller.
Its calm opening is twice broken by a stormy con fuoco episode.

15/2.about: A delicately ornamented F-sharp major melody, laced with filigree turns and triplets, gives way to a quicker, more agitated central episode before the opening returns in an even more elaborately decorated guise.
15/2.ctx: The second of the Op. 15 nocturnes and, alongside the Op. 9 No. 2, one of Chopin’s most popular in the genre during his own lifetime. It shares the set’s dedication to Ferdinand Hiller.
facts: The second of the three Op. 15 nocturnes.
Among the most admired of Chopin’s nocturnes in his own lifetime.
Richly decorated with turns and triplet figuration.

15/3.about: An unusual, restless nocturne that opens with a languid, mazurka-tinged melody in G minor before turning, without transition, into a hushed, chorale-like religioso passage in G major — a structural experiment unlike any other nocturne Chopin wrote.
15/3.ctx: The last of the Op. 15 set, composed in 1833 and originally intended to accompany a reading of Shakespeare’s Hamlet, though Chopin removed that association before publication. Its blend of Polish dance rhythm and devotional chorale makes it the most idiosyncratic of the three.
facts: Originally associated with Shakespeare’s Hamlet, a link Chopin later suppressed.
Combines a mazurka-like opening with a hymn-like religioso close.
The third of the Op. 15 nocturnes.

27/1.about: A dark, brooding nocturne in C-sharp minor that unfolds over wide, murmuring left-hand arpeggios, building steadily from hushed unease to a passionate, full-voiced climax before subsiding into the shadows once more.
27/1.ctx: The first of the two Op. 27 nocturnes, composed in 1835 and dedicated, with its companion, to the Countess d’Appony. It marks a new depth of drama in the genre, moving well beyond the salon character of Chopin’s earlier nocturnes.
facts: The first of the two Op. 27 nocturnes.
Dedicated, with its companion, to the Countess d’Appony.
One of the darkest and most dramatic of Chopin’s nocturnes.

32/1.about: A gentle, hymn-like B major melody unfolds with deceptive calm, only for the nocturne to end abruptly with a startling, recitative-like coda in the minor — a dramatic subversion of the genre’s usual peaceful close.
32/1.ctx: The first of the two Op. 32 nocturnes, composed in 1836–37 and dedicated to Madame de Billing. Its jarring ending was singled out by early listeners as a striking break from convention.
facts: The first of the two Op. 32 nocturnes.
Dedicated to Madame de Billing.
Ends with a sudden, unsettling minor-key coda.

32/2.about: A tender A-flat major nocturne framed by a brief introduction, its lyrical main theme growing more agitated in a turbulent middle section before the opening melody returns, now touched with unrest.
32/2.ctx: The second of the Op. 32 nocturnes, composed alongside its companion in 1836–37 and published the following year. Its combination of tenderness and agitation looks forward to the more dramatic nocturnes of Chopin’s middle years.
facts: The second of the two Op. 32 nocturnes.
Composed in 1836–37.
Framed by a short introductory phrase.

37/1.about: A melancholy G minor melody alternates with a hushed, chorale-like passage in the major, the two ideas trading places as the nocturne unfolds, closing quietly in the minor.
37/1.ctx: The first of the two Op. 37 nocturnes, begun in 1838 around the time of Chopin’s journey to Majorca with George Sand. Its chorale-like interludes reflect the increasing harmonic and textural experimentation of his middle years.
facts: The first of the two Op. 37 nocturnes.
Composed around the time of Chopin’s trip to Majorca.
Alternates a melancholy theme with a chorale-like passage.

37/2.about: A barcarolle-like nocturne built from flowing parallel sixths that suggest the gentle rocking of a boat, framing a more songful central melody, all in a warm G major.
37/2.ctx: The second of the Op. 37 nocturnes, completed in 1839 during Chopin’s first summer at George Sand’s estate at Nohant. Its rocking, water-borne character anticipates the Barcarolle, Op. 60, that he would write several years later.
facts: The second of the two Op. 37 nocturnes.
Its rocking sixths anticipate the later Barcarolle, Op. 60.
Completed at Nohant in 1839.

48/1.about: A grand, tragic nocturne that rises from a slow, funereal C minor lament, through a grave chorale marked doppio movimento, to a turbulent, agitato climax of octaves before the opening lament returns, now overwhelmed.
48/1.ctx: The first of the Op. 48 nocturnes, widely regarded as the most powerful and large-scaled of the entire series, composed in 1841 and dedicated to Laure Duperré. Its scope and drama push the nocturne far beyond its salon origins.
facts: The first of the two Op. 48 nocturnes.
Considered the grandest and most dramatic of all Chopin’s nocturnes.
Dedicated to Laure Duperré.

48/2.about: An introspective F-sharp minor nocturne whose songful outer sections frame a hushed, recitative-like middle section, its irregular, speech-like rhythms making it one of Chopin’s most unusual and searching slow movements.
48/2.ctx: The second of the Op. 48 nocturnes, composed alongside its companion in 1841. Its meditative, almost improvisatory middle section was reportedly inspired by Chopin’s advice to a pupil to imagine a tyrant’s despotic command answered by a plea for mercy.
facts: The second of the two Op. 48 nocturnes.
Its middle section has an unusually speech-like, recitative quality.
Composed in 1841.

55/1.about: A simple, plaintive melody in F minor unfolds with restrained sadness before the texture thickens into a turbulent, triplet-filled close, the calm of the opening never quite regained.
55/1.ctx: The first of the two Op. 55 nocturnes, composed between 1842 and 1844 and dedicated to Chopin’s pupil Jane Stirling, who later helped arrange his final tour of Britain. Its unresolved, darkening ending is characteristic of his late style.
facts: The first of the two Op. 55 nocturnes.
Dedicated to Jane Stirling, Chopin’s devoted pupil.
Ends in an unresolved, darkly turbulent mood.

55/2.about: A flowing, contrapuntal nocturne in E-flat major built from long, elaborately ornamented melodic lines that weave between the hands in a texture closer to a duet than a single melody with accompaniment.
55/2.ctx: The second of the Op. 55 nocturnes, composed alongside its companion and, like it, dedicated to Jane Stirling. Its intricate two-part counterpoint shows Chopin’s late fascination with Bach, whose keyboard music he taught to his pupils.
facts: The second of the two Op. 55 nocturnes.
Its two flowing melodic lines suggest a duet rather than melody and accompaniment.
Reflects Chopin’s late interest in Bach’s counterpoint.

62/1.about: A late, richly ornamented nocturne in B major whose long trills and decorated melodic lines create an almost improvisatory, veiled texture, interrupted by a more troubled middle section before the opening serenity returns.
62/1.ctx: The first of the two Op. 62 nocturnes, composed in 1846, the last full year Chopin spent at Nohant with George Sand before their relationship ended. It was dedicated to his pupil Mademoiselle R. de Konneritz.
facts: The first of the two Op. 62 nocturnes.
One of the last works Chopin composed at Nohant.
Its melody is decorated with long, veiling trills.

62/2.about: A late nocturne of serene, songful lyricism in E major framing a more agitated, contrapuntally dense central section, its two moods held in careful balance across a compact span.
62/2.ctx: The second of the Op. 62 nocturnes, composed alongside its companion in 1846. Together the two mark the final appearance of the nocturne in Chopin’s output, their combination of serenity and unease characteristic of his last completed years.
facts: The second of the two Op. 62 nocturnes.
The last nocturnes Chopin published in his lifetime.
Composed in 1846 at Nohant.

72/1.about: A youthful nocturne in E minor with a heartfelt, simply accompanied melody over flowing broken chords, more modest in scope than Chopin’s later nocturnes but already recognisably his voice.
72/1.ctx: Composed around 1827, when Chopin was still a teenager in Warsaw, and published only in 1855, six years after his death, as part of a posthumous collection assembled by Julian Fontana. It is the earliest of all his nocturnes.
facts: The earliest nocturne Chopin is known to have written.
Composed while he was still a teenager in Warsaw.
Published posthumously in 1855 by Julian Fontana.

posth-c.about: A brief, sombre nocturne in C minor, plain and unadorned by comparison with Chopin’s published nocturnes, its simple melody and dark harmony giving it an intimate, private character.
posth-c.ctx: Composed around 1837 but never published or performed during Chopin’s lifetime, the manuscript surfaced only in the twentieth century and was first published in 1938, nearly ninety years after his death.
facts: Not published until 1938, almost ninety years after Chopin’s death.
One of the plainest and least ornamented of his nocturnes.
Composed around 1837.

10/1.about: A study in spanning arpeggios, the right hand sweeping across almost the entire keyboard in constant broken chords while the left hand holds a slow, majestic bass melody — an étude on reach and sonority as much as technique.
10/1.ctx: The opening study of Op. 10, composed in 1829 and dedicated, with the whole set, to Franz Liszt. Its grand, cascading sound announces Chopin’s ambition to reimagine the étude as a work of art rather than mere finger drill.
facts: Opens the set of twelve études, Op. 10.
Dedicated, with the whole opus, to Franz Liszt.
A study in wide, spanning right-hand arpeggios.

10/2.about: A chromatic scale study for the weak outer fingers of the right hand, which must pick out a running chromatic line while the thumb and index finger simultaneously hold an inner melodic voice.
10/2.ctx: The second of the Op. 10 études, composed in 1829, when Chopin was still a student in Warsaw. It targets the third, fourth and fifth fingers specifically, a technical problem few composers before him had isolated so precisely.
facts: Isolates the weaker outer fingers of the right hand.
One of the most purely technical of the twelve études.
Composed in 1829, before Chopin left Warsaw.

10/4.about: A fierce, headlong torrent of semiquavers passed rapidly between the hands, its relentless momentum and driving energy making it one of the most exhilarating and outwardly virtuosic of the set.
10/4.ctx: The fourth of the Op. 10 études, composed around 1832 shortly after Chopin’s arrival in Paris. Its breathless velocity has made it one of the most frequently programmed of all twelve studies.
facts: Among the fastest and most outwardly virtuosic of the Op. 10 études.
Its figuration passes rapidly between the two hands.
Composed shortly after Chopin settled in Paris.

10/6.about: A brooding, chromatically wandering study in sustained legato, in which an inner voice must sing out smoothly through a web of continuously moving harmony, testing the pianist’s control of tone as much as fingers.
10/6.ctx: The sixth of the Op. 10 études, composed around 1830. Unlike the more obviously virtuosic studies around it, its challenge is almost entirely one of sustained cantabile touch and harmonic control.
facts: A study in legato tone rather than outward virtuosity.
Its harmony shifts chromatically throughout.
Composed around 1830, before Chopin left Poland.

10/7.about: A bright, toccata-like study in rapid alternating double notes, its crisp, repeated-note figuration demanding evenness and lightness of touch across constantly shifting hand positions.
10/7.ctx: The seventh of the Op. 10 études, composed around 1832. Its glittering surface and compact energy make it one of the more good-humoured studies of the set.
facts: A study in rapid alternating double notes.
Composed around 1832, soon after Chopin’s move to Paris.
One of the brighter, more good-humoured études of Op. 10.

10/8.about: A brilliant study in cascading right-hand passagework over a cheerful, striding left-hand melody, its bright F major sound and unflagging energy making it one of the most extroverted of the twelve.
10/8.ctx: The eighth of the Op. 10 études, composed in 1829 while Chopin was still a student. Its sparkling figuration and sunny character offer a moment of relief among the set’s darker and more introspective studies.
facts: One of the sunniest and most extroverted of the Op. 10 études.
Composed in 1829, among the earliest of the set.
Combines rapid right-hand passagework with a striding bass melody.

10/9.about: An agitated study in wide left-hand stretches and leaps beneath a restless, syncopated right-hand melody, its turbulent character and unstable harmony giving it an unusually dark, anxious mood for the set.
10/9.ctx: The ninth of the Op. 10 études, composed in 1829. Its focus on the left hand’s reach and agility anticipates the more famous left-hand study, No. 12, that closes the opus.
facts: A study focused on the left hand’s stretch and agility.
Composed in 1829, during Chopin’s student years.
One of the more turbulent and anxious of the Op. 10 études.

10/10.about: A sparkling study in constantly varied articulation and shifting hand positions, alternating staccato and legato figures across wide leaps, prized by pianists as one of the most purely delightful of the twelve.
10/10.ctx: The tenth of the Op. 10 études, composed in 1829. Anton Rubinstein reportedly called it the study he would most like to have written, admiring its combination of technical demand with effortless musical charm.
facts: Anton Rubinstein reportedly admired it above all the other études.
A study in constantly shifting articulation and hand position.
Composed in 1829, among Chopin’s student works.

10/11.about: A harp-like study built from widely spread, rolled chords in both hands, its arpeggiated textures and resonant pedalling creating a shimmering wash of sound rather than a driving melodic line.
10/11.ctx: The eleventh of the Op. 10 études, composed in 1829. Its broken-chord textures, spanning the full width of the keyboard, look forward to the sonorous, coloristic piano writing of later composers such as Debussy.
facts: A study in widely spread, arpeggiated chords.
Its resonant, harp-like sound anticipates later Impressionist piano writing.
Composed in 1829, near the start of the Op. 10 project.

25/1.about: A gently flowing melody floats above continuous rippling, harp-like arpeggios spread across both hands, its soft dynamic and warm A-flat major harmony giving it the nickname ‘Aeolian Harp’ or ‘Shepherd Boy’.
25/1.ctx: The opening étude of Op. 25, composed in 1836 and dedicated, with the whole set, to Marie d’Agoult, Franz Liszt’s companion. Robert Schumann praised it for its poetic, wind-blown atmosphere.
facts: Opens the twelve études of Op. 25.
Nicknamed ‘Aeolian Harp’ for its rippling, wind-like arpeggios.
Dedicated, with the whole opus, to Marie d’Agoult.

25/2.about: A whispering, rapid triplet figure runs continuously beneath a slower-moving melodic line, the two rhythms overlapping in a subtly disorienting cross-current that gives the étude its restless, murmuring character.
25/2.ctx: The second of the Op. 25 études, composed in 1836. Schumann described its effect as like a swarm of tiny notes swirling around a simple, calm melody, a vivid picture of its rhythmic layering.
facts: A study in overlapping triplet and duple rhythms.
Schumann likened its texture to a swarm of tiny notes.
Composed in 1836, alongside the rest of Op. 25.

25/3.about: A light, dancing study built from intricate, syncopated rhythmic figures tossed between the hands, its playful unpredictability and quick tempo giving it a scherzo-like character within the set.
25/3.ctx: The third of the Op. 25 études, among the earliest composed, dating from around 1834. Its rhythmic games and light touch offer contrast to the more overtly virtuosic studies that surround it.
facts: A study in intricate, syncopated cross-rhythms.
Among the earliest of the Op. 25 études to be composed.
Has a light, scherzo-like character.

25/4.about: Staccato leaps in the left hand punctuate a syncopated, off-beat melody in the right, the combination demanding precision and a light wrist across constant, unpredictable jumps.
25/4.ctx: The fourth of the Op. 25 études, composed in the early 1830s. Its jagged rhythmic profile and reliance on staccato leaps make it a study in agility and rhythmic independence between the hands.
facts: A study in staccato leaps and syncopated rhythm.
Composed in the early 1830s.
Demands rhythmic independence between the two hands.

25/5.about: A capricious opening built from biting grace-note figures and dissonant appoggiaturas gives way, in its middle section, to a broad, singing E major melody, one of Chopin’s most gorgeous, before the acid opening returns.
25/5.ctx: The fifth of the Op. 25 études, composed around 1832. Its harsh, almost mocking outer sections framing a melody of ravishing lyricism have earned it the nickname ‘Wrong Note’.
facts: Sometimes nicknamed the ‘Wrong Note’ étude for its biting dissonances.
Its middle section contains one of Chopin’s most lyrical melodies.
Composed around 1832.

25/6.about: A notorious study in rapid right-hand thirds, in which both notes of every interval must be played with equal clarity and speed, making it one of the most feared technical challenges in the entire piano repertoire.
25/6.ctx: The sixth of the Op. 25 études, composed in the early 1830s. Its unrelenting double-note writing has made it a byword among pianists for a specific and exceptionally demanding technical problem.
facts: Widely regarded as one of the hardest études for playing thirds.
A pure technical study in double notes.
Composed in the early 1830s.

25/7.about: A slow, deeply expressive study built around a cello-like melody in the left hand, singing beneath a more decorative right-hand line, the two voices forming an intimate, melancholy duet.
25/7.ctx: The seventh of the Op. 25 études, composed in 1836. Its unusually slow tempo and songful left-hand melody make it closer in spirit to a nocturne than to the virtuoso studies around it.
facts: Built on a singing, cello-like melody in the left hand.
One of the slowest and most lyrical of all the études.
Composed in 1836.

25/8.about: A flowing study in legato sixths, both hands moving in parallel through continuously shifting harmony, its smooth surface concealing the considerable finger independence required to keep every voice singing.
25/8.ctx: The eighth of the Op. 25 études, composed in 1836. Its focus on sixths complements the study in thirds, Op. 25 No. 6, as one of the set’s two great interval studies.
facts: A study in parallel sixths, complementing the étude in thirds.
Composed in 1836, with the rest of Op. 25.
Demands smooth legato across constantly shifting harmony.

25/10.about: A thunderous octave study whose relentless outer sections, full of leaping, hammered octaves, frame a more lyrical middle section of songful, sustained melody — one of the most physically demanding of all the études.
25/10.ctx: The tenth of the Op. 25 études, composed around 1832. Its combination of brute octave technique with a passage of real tenderness at its centre makes it one of the most dramatically effective studies Chopin wrote.
facts: A study in rapid, leaping octaves.
One of the most physically strenuous of all Chopin’s études.
Its middle section offers a contrasting lyrical episode.

25/12.about: Surging arpeggios rise and fall in both hands together across the full span of the keyboard, evoking crashing waves and giving the étude its nickname ‘Ocean’; it closes the Op. 25 set in a blaze of C minor energy.
25/12.ctx: The last of the Op. 25 études, composed in 1836. Its sweeping, symmetrical figuration in both hands makes it a fitting, monumental close to the second book of studies.
facts: Nicknamed the ‘Ocean’ étude for its surging, wave-like arpeggios.
Closes the twelve études of Op. 25.
Built on figuration shared symmetrically between both hands.

nouv/1.about: A gentle study in cross-rhythms of three notes against two, its calm, flowing surface concealing the subtle coordination needed to keep both rhythmic streams perfectly even.
nouv/1.ctx: The first of the Trois nouvelles études, composed around 1839 for inclusion in the Méthode des méthodes de piano, a piano method compiled by Ignaz Moscheles and François-Joseph Fétis, at their invitation.
facts: Written for a piano method by Moscheles and Fétis.
A study in three-against-two cross-rhythms.
One of three studies Chopin wrote outside his two main opuses of études.

nouv/2.about: A graceful study in similar cross-rhythmic polyrhythms to its companion, its lilting melody floating over a gently syncopated accompaniment in A-flat major.
nouv/2.ctx: The second of the Trois nouvelles études, composed alongside its companions in 1839 for Moscheles and Fétis’s piano method. Its warmth and lyricism make it the most immediately winning of the three.
facts: The second of the Trois nouvelles études.
Composed for the same piano method as its companions.
Its melody has an unusually lilting, songlike grace.

nouv/3.about: A calm, songful study that moves legato and staccato within the same hand simultaneously, requiring the fingers of one hand to separate two different touches at once.
nouv/3.ctx: The third and final of the Trois nouvelles études, completed in 1839 for the Moscheles–Fétis method. Its technical problem, dividing a single hand between two articulations, is unlike anything in Chopin’s two main sets of études.
facts: Requires legato and staccato touch within a single hand at once.
The last of the Trois nouvelles études.
Composed for Moscheles and Fétis’s piano method in 1839.

28/1.about: A brief, agitated burst of rising, syncopated figures in C major, its restless energy setting an ecstatic, unsettled tone for the whole cycle to come.
28/1.ctx: Composed mostly during the winter of 1838–39 that Chopin spent with George Sand and her children on Majorca, and finished in Paris; the set of twenty-four preludes, Op. 28, was published in 1839 with a dual dedication to Chopin’s friend the pianist Joseph Christoph Kessler and, in the French edition, to the piano-maker Camille Pleyel. It opens the set of twenty-four preludes in all major and minor keys.
facts: Opens the cycle of twenty-four preludes.
Marked Agitato.
One of the shortest preludes in the set.

28/2.about: A stark, dissonant lament in A minor, its bare, creeping bass line and unresolved harmony giving it a bleak, unsettled atmosphere unlike anything Chopin had written before.
28/2.ctx: Composed mostly during the winter of 1838–39 that Chopin spent with George Sand and her children on Majorca, and finished in Paris; the set of twenty-four preludes, Op. 28, was published in 1839 with a dual dedication to Chopin’s friend the pianist Joseph Christoph Kessler and, in the French edition, to the piano-maker Camille Pleyel. Its harmonic ambiguity struck contemporaries as almost shockingly modern for its time.
facts: Its harmony is unusually bare and unresolved for its era.
Marked Lento.
Considered one of the most harmonically daring preludes.

28/3.about: Fleet, rippling left-hand triplets run beneath a simple, bright melody in G major, the prelude’s light touch offering a moment of calm after the darkness of its predecessor.
28/3.ctx: Composed mostly during the winter of 1838–39 that Chopin spent with George Sand and her children on Majorca, and finished in Paris; the set of twenty-four preludes, Op. 28, was published in 1839 with a dual dedication to Chopin’s friend the pianist Joseph Christoph Kessler and, in the French edition, to the piano-maker Camille Pleyel. Its quick, effortless charm makes it one of the most immediately appealing of the set.
facts: Marked Vivace.
Built on continuous left-hand triplet figuration.
One of the lightest and brightest of the twenty-four preludes.

28/4.about: A mournful melody unfolds over slowly, chromatically shifting chords in E minor — this is the prelude that was played at Chopin’s own funeral, alongside Mozart’s Requiem.
28/4.ctx: Composed mostly during the winter of 1838–39 that Chopin spent with George Sand and her children on Majorca, and finished in Paris; the set of twenty-four preludes, Op. 28, was published in 1839 with a dual dedication to Chopin’s friend the pianist Joseph Christoph Kessler and, in the French edition, to the piano-maker Camille Pleyel. Its slow, descending chromatic bass has made it one of the most famous single pages of Romantic piano music.
facts: Played at Chopin’s funeral in 1849.
Marked Largo.
Its chromatically descending bass line is one of the most imitated gestures in piano music.

28/5.about: A quick, delicate web of interlocking figures moves swiftly through D major, its brevity and lightness making it one of the most fleeting preludes of the cycle.
28/5.ctx: Composed mostly during the winter of 1838–39 that Chopin spent with George Sand and her children on Majorca, and finished in Paris; the set of twenty-four preludes, Op. 28, was published in 1839 with a dual dedication to Chopin’s friend the pianist Joseph Christoph Kessler and, in the French edition, to the piano-maker Camille Pleyel. Its rapid tempo and airy texture contrast sharply with the funereal prelude that precedes it.
facts: Marked Allegro molto.
One of the briefest preludes in the set.
Built from continuously interlocking melodic fragments.

28/6.about: A cello-like melody sings in the left hand beneath a quiet, gently pulsing right-hand accompaniment, the B minor prelude unfolding as an intimate, understated lament.
28/6.ctx: Composed mostly during the winter of 1838–39 that Chopin spent with George Sand and her children on Majorca, and finished in Paris; the set of twenty-four preludes, Op. 28, was published in 1839 with a dual dedication to Chopin’s friend the pianist Joseph Christoph Kessler and, in the French edition, to the piano-maker Camille Pleyel. George Sand’s son Maurice reportedly admired this prelude above the others, and Chopin is said to have particularly loved it himself.
facts: Built on a singing, cello-like left-hand melody.
Marked Lento assai.
Reportedly one of Chopin’s own favourites among the set.

28/7.about: A tiny, mazurka-like miniature of just sixteen bars, its simple, graceful melody in A major making it the shortest and most immediately charming prelude of the entire cycle.
28/7.ctx: Composed mostly during the winter of 1838–39 that Chopin spent with George Sand and her children on Majorca, and finished in Paris; the set of twenty-four preludes, Op. 28, was published in 1839 with a dual dedication to Chopin’s friend the pianist Joseph Christoph Kessler and, in the French edition, to the piano-maker Camille Pleyel. Its brevity and dance-like lilt made it instantly popular, and it has been arranged and quoted more often than almost any other prelude.
facts: The shortest of the twenty-four preludes.
Has the rhythm of a Polish mazurka.
One of the most frequently quoted and arranged of Chopin’s pieces.

28/8.about: Stormy, dense chromatic figuration churns beneath an urgent, searching melody in F-sharp minor, the prelude building to considerable intensity within its brief span.
28/8.ctx: Composed mostly during the winter of 1838–39 that Chopin spent with George Sand and her children on Majorca, and finished in Paris; the set of twenty-four preludes, Op. 28, was published in 1839 with a dual dedication to Chopin’s friend the pianist Joseph Christoph Kessler and, in the French edition, to the piano-maker Camille Pleyel. Its restless chromaticism and dense texture make it one of the more technically demanding preludes despite its short length.
facts: Marked Molto agitato.
Built on dense chromatic figuration.
One of the more technically demanding of the shorter preludes.

28/9.about: A solemn, grand processional in dotted rhythms and thick chords, its brief, hymn-like grandeur in E major giving it an almost orchestral weight despite lasting barely half a minute.
28/9.ctx: Composed mostly during the winter of 1838–39 that Chopin spent with George Sand and her children on Majorca, and finished in Paris; the set of twenty-four preludes, Op. 28, was published in 1839 with a dual dedication to Chopin’s friend the pianist Joseph Christoph Kessler and, in the French edition, to the piano-maker Camille Pleyel. Its massive, chordal sonority packed into so short a span has led some to compare its scale to a much larger work.
facts: Marked Largo.
Built almost entirely from thick, dotted-rhythm chords.
One of the most compact yet weighty of the preludes.

28/10.about: Brief, flickering descending runs in the right hand are answered by a dotted, mazurka-like rhythm in the left, the C-sharp minor prelude passing in a flash of light and shadow.
28/10.ctx: Composed mostly during the winter of 1838–39 that Chopin spent with George Sand and her children on Majorca, and finished in Paris; the set of twenty-four preludes, Op. 28, was published in 1839 with a dual dedication to Chopin’s friend the pianist Joseph Christoph Kessler and, in the French edition, to the piano-maker Camille Pleyel. Its quick alternation of scale-work and dance rhythm makes it one of the more capricious preludes of the set.
facts: Marked Allegro molto.
Combines rapid scale-work with a mazurka-like rhythm.
One of the briefest preludes in the cycle.

28/11.about: Quick, graceful and fleeting, this B major prelude dances lightly through triplet figures with an easy, untroubled charm, over almost before it begins.
28/11.ctx: Composed mostly during the winter of 1838–39 that Chopin spent with George Sand and her children on Majorca, and finished in Paris; the set of twenty-four preludes, Op. 28, was published in 1839 with a dual dedication to Chopin’s friend the pianist Joseph Christoph Kessler and, in the French edition, to the piano-maker Camille Pleyel. Its light touch and brevity offer a moment of relaxation amid the more intense preludes surrounding it.
facts: Marked Vivace.
One of the lightest and most graceful preludes.
Lasts under a minute in performance.

28/12.about: Galloping, chromatic turmoil drives this G-sharp minor prelude forward without pause, its constant triplet motion and dark harmony giving it a restless, headlong energy.
28/12.ctx: Composed mostly during the winter of 1838–39 that Chopin spent with George Sand and her children on Majorca, and finished in Paris; the set of twenty-four preludes, Op. 28, was published in 1839 with a dual dedication to Chopin’s friend the pianist Joseph Christoph Kessler and, in the French edition, to the piano-maker Camille Pleyel. Its relentless momentum makes it one of the more virtuosic and technically taxing of the shorter preludes.
facts: Marked Presto.
Built on continuous galloping triplet figuration.
One of the fastest and most turbulent preludes in the set.

28/13.about: A tranquil, nocturne-like song in F-sharp major, its long, gently flowing melody and warm harmony giving it a serene calm before a brief, more troubled middle episode.
28/13.ctx: Composed mostly during the winter of 1838–39 that Chopin spent with George Sand and her children on Majorca, and finished in Paris; the set of twenty-four preludes, Op. 28, was published in 1839 with a dual dedication to Chopin’s friend the pianist Joseph Christoph Kessler and, in the French edition, to the piano-maker Camille Pleyel. Its songful, nocturne-like character sets it apart from the more compact, aphoristic preludes that surround it.
facts: Marked Lento.
Closer in character to a nocturne than to the shorter preludes around it.
One of the longer pieces in the cycle.

28/14.about: Brief, stormy unison triplets rumble through both hands together in E-flat minor, the whole prelude passing in a low, ominous murmur that never quite resolves into a clear melody.
28/14.ctx: Composed mostly during the winter of 1838–39 that Chopin spent with George Sand and her children on Majorca, and finished in Paris; the set of twenty-four preludes, Op. 28, was published in 1839 with a dual dedication to Chopin’s friend the pianist Joseph Christoph Kessler and, in the French edition, to the piano-maker Camille Pleyel. Its unison writing, with both hands moving together in the same rhythm, is unusual within the set and gives it an eerie, faceless quality.
facts: Both hands play in rhythmic unison throughout.
Marked Allegro.
One of the darkest and most understated preludes.

28/16.about: A fiery, virtuosic torrent in B-flat minor, its relentless right-hand cascades tumbling over pounding left-hand chords in one of the most technically ferocious preludes of the whole set.
28/16.ctx: Composed mostly during the winter of 1838–39 that Chopin spent with George Sand and her children on Majorca, and finished in Paris; the set of twenty-four preludes, Op. 28, was published in 1839 with a dual dedication to Chopin’s friend the pianist Joseph Christoph Kessler and, in the French edition, to the piano-maker Camille Pleyel. Its breakneck speed and difficulty make it, alongside No. 24, one of the two most demanding preludes to perform.
facts: Marked Presto con fuoco.
One of the two most technically demanding preludes, with No. 24.
Built on relentless cascading right-hand figuration.

28/17.about: A warm, romantic song in A-flat major, its broad melody accompanied by a bell-like low note that tolls quietly through much of the coda, an effect Chopin is said to have based on a real bell he once heard.
28/17.ctx: Composed mostly during the winter of 1838–39 that Chopin spent with George Sand and her children on Majorca, and finished in Paris; the set of twenty-four preludes, Op. 28, was published in 1839 with a dual dedication to Chopin’s friend the pianist Joseph Christoph Kessler and, in the French edition, to the piano-maker Camille Pleyel. Mendelssohn reportedly told Chopin how much he admired this particular prelude, singling it out among the whole set.
facts: Mendelssohn is said to have particularly admired this prelude.
Features a repeated, bell-like tolling note in the coda.
One of the warmest and most lyrical preludes in the set.

28/18.about: Dramatic, recitative-like outbursts in F minor alternate with sudden silences, the prelude built almost entirely from bold, speech-like gestures rather than continuous melody.
28/18.ctx: Composed mostly during the winter of 1838–39 that Chopin spent with George Sand and her children on Majorca, and finished in Paris; the set of twenty-four preludes, Op. 28, was published in 1839 with a dual dedication to Chopin’s friend the pianist Joseph Christoph Kessler and, in the French edition, to the piano-maker Camille Pleyel. Its fragmented, declamatory writing gives it an operatic, almost vocal quality unlike any other prelude in the set.
facts: Marked Allegro molto.
Built from dramatic, speech-like fragments rather than continuous melody.
One of the most declamatory preludes in the cycle.

28/19.about: Wide, graceful leaps carry a flowing triplet melody across the keyboard in E-flat major, the hands spanning large distances in an elegant, soaring texture.
28/19.ctx: Composed mostly during the winter of 1838–39 that Chopin spent with George Sand and her children on Majorca, and finished in Paris; the set of twenty-four preludes, Op. 28, was published in 1839 with a dual dedication to Chopin’s friend the pianist Joseph Christoph Kessler and, in the French edition, to the piano-maker Camille Pleyel. Its wide-spanning figuration requires considerable reach and technical facility from the performer.
facts: Marked Vivace.
Requires wide leaps and reach across the keyboard.
One of the more technically demanding shorter preludes.

28/20.about: Solemn, funeral-march chords in C minor, stark and unadorned, pass by in barely thirteen bars, their simple weight later borrowed by Rachmaninoff as the theme for a famous set of variations.
28/20.ctx: Composed mostly during the winter of 1838–39 that Chopin spent with George Sand and her children on Majorca, and finished in Paris; the set of twenty-four preludes, Op. 28, was published in 1839 with a dual dedication to Chopin’s friend the pianist Joseph Christoph Kessler and, in the French edition, to the piano-maker Camille Pleyel. Its stark simplicity and dark grandeur made it one of the most instantly recognisable of all the preludes, and its theme has been reused by later composers including Rachmaninoff and Busoni.
facts: Rachmaninoff based his Op. 22 Variations on this prelude’s theme.
One of the shortest yet most famous of the twenty-four preludes.
Built entirely from stark, unadorned chords.

28/21.about: A lyrical, singing melody in B-flat major unfolds over a gradually expanding, richly voiced accompaniment, the prelude growing warmer and more elaborate as it proceeds.
28/21.ctx: Composed mostly during the winter of 1838–39 that Chopin spent with George Sand and her children on Majorca, and finished in Paris; the set of twenty-four preludes, Op. 28, was published in 1839 with a dual dedication to Chopin’s friend the pianist Joseph Christoph Kessler and, in the French edition, to the piano-maker Camille Pleyel. Its long-breathed melodic writing gives it a songlike quality closer to the nocturnes than to the more aphoristic preludes nearby.
facts: Marked Cantabile.
Its accompaniment grows steadily richer as the piece unfolds.
One of the more lyrical, songlike preludes in the set.

28/22.about: Defiant octaves hammer out a driving melody in the left hand beneath agitated right-hand figuration, the G minor prelude building to a forceful, uncompromising close.
28/22.ctx: Composed mostly during the winter of 1838–39 that Chopin spent with George Sand and her children on Majorca, and finished in Paris; the set of twenty-four preludes, Op. 28, was published in 1839 with a dual dedication to Chopin’s friend the pianist Joseph Christoph Kessler and, in the French edition, to the piano-maker Camille Pleyel. Its combative left-hand octaves make it one of the more physically demanding preludes of the set.
facts: Marked Molto agitato.
Built on driving octaves in the left hand.
One of the more technically strenuous preludes.

28/23.about: Light, shimmering filigree runs through F major in constant, sparkling motion, the prelude ending on an unresolved dominant seventh that leaves the harmony hanging, unclosed.
28/23.ctx: Composed mostly during the winter of 1838–39 that Chopin spent with George Sand and her children on Majorca, and finished in Paris; the set of twenty-four preludes, Op. 28, was published in 1839 with a dual dedication to Chopin’s friend the pianist Joseph Christoph Kessler and, in the French edition, to the piano-maker Camille Pleyel. Its ambiguous, unresolved ending was noted by early listeners as a striking, almost modern touch.
facts: Ends on an unresolved dominant seventh chord.
Marked Moderato.
One of the most harmonically open-ended of the preludes.

28/24.about: A tempestuous D minor finale of driving, unrelenting energy, ending with three low, hammered notes struck fortissimo — a stark, defiant close to the entire cycle.
28/24.ctx: Composed mostly during the winter of 1838–39 that Chopin spent with George Sand and her children on Majorca, and finished in Paris; the set of twenty-four preludes, Op. 28, was published in 1839 with a dual dedication to Chopin’s friend the pianist Joseph Christoph Kessler and, in the French edition, to the piano-maker Camille Pleyel. Its ferocious difficulty and dramatic close make it a fitting climax to the set, and it is often singled out as the most overtly virtuosic of all twenty-four preludes.
facts: Closes the cycle of twenty-four preludes.
Ends with three hammered fortissimo notes in the bass.
Regarded as the most virtuosic prelude of the entire set.

45.about: A standalone prelude outside the Op. 28 cycle, its dreamy, chromatically modulating arpeggios wandering through distant keys before a brief, improvisatory cadenza leads back to a hushed close in C-sharp major.
45.ctx: Composed in 1841, two years after the Op. 28 set, and dedicated to Princess Elizaveta Czernicheva. Its wandering harmony and improvisatory cadenza make it more exploratory and rhapsodic than any of the twenty-four preludes.
facts: Composed separately from, and after, the Op. 28 cycle.
Dedicated to Princess Elizaveta Czernicheva.
Its wandering harmony passes through unusually distant keys.

34/1.about: A brilliant concert waltz with an extended, fanfare-like introduction before its sweeping A-flat major main theme, closing with a glittering, virtuosic coda far removed from the ballroom.
34/1.ctx: The first of the three Op. 34 waltzes, composed in 1835 and dedicated to Mademoiselle de Thun-Hohenstein. Chopin called these three pieces ‘valses brillantes’, concert waltzes meant for listening rather than dancing.
facts: The first of the three Op. 34 waltzes.
Chopin labelled the set ‘valses brillantes’.
Dedicated to Mademoiselle de Thun-Hohenstein.

34/3.about: A whirling, breathless waltz in F major of spinning, unbroken motion, sometimes nicknamed the ‘Cat Waltz’ for a popular but apocryphal story that its rapid final descent depicts a cat leaping across the keys.
34/3.ctx: The last of the Op. 34 waltzes, composed in 1838. Its perpetual-motion energy and abrupt ending have made the ‘Cat Waltz’ nickname persist in popular imagination, however unlikely its origin.
facts: Sometimes nicknamed the ‘Cat Waltz’.
The last of the three Op. 34 waltzes.
Built on continuous, unbroken spinning motion.

42.about: A grand waltz whose melody moves in duple groupings against the triple waltz bass, opening with a long trill that leads into a texture of shifting cross-rhythms unusual for the genre, before closing in a blaze of virtuosic energy.
42.ctx: Composed in 1840, this waltz is often considered the most sophisticated and musically substantial of all Chopin’s waltzes, its rhythmic complexity elevating it well above the conventional salon dance.
facts: Its melody moves in twos against a waltz bass in threes.
Opens with an extended trill.
Regarded as the most musically ambitious of Chopin’s waltzes.

64/2.about: A wistful waltz that alternates a melancholy C-sharp minor theme with a whirling, faster refrain in the major, its shifting moods making it one of the most emotionally varied of all the waltzes.
64/2.ctx: The second of the Op. 64 waltzes, composed alongside its famous companion the ‘Minute Waltz’ and dedicated, with the set, to Countess Delfina Potocka. It remains one of Chopin’s most performed and beloved waltzes.
facts: The second of the three Op. 64 waltzes.
Dedicated, with the set, to Countess Delfina Potocka.
One of Chopin’s most frequently performed waltzes.

64/3.about: A graceful, gently modulating waltz in A-flat major, its melody wandering through unexpected harmonic shifts with an easy elegance typical of Chopin’s late style.
64/3.ctx: The last of the Op. 64 waltzes, composed in 1846–47, among the final works Chopin published in his lifetime. Its subtlety and harmonic finesse mark the mature culmination of his approach to the genre.
facts: The last of the three Op. 64 waltzes.
Among the final works Chopin published before his death.
Notable for its subtle, wandering harmony.

69/1.about: A tender farewell waltz in A-flat major, its warm, sighing melody carrying an unmistakable note of parting sentiment.
69/1.ctx: Composed in 1835 for Maria Wodzińska, a young woman Chopin was briefly engaged to marry, and published posthumously in 1855 with the added title ‘L’Adieu’ referencing their parting.
facts: Written for Maria Wodzińska, to whom Chopin was briefly engaged.
Published posthumously with the title ‘L’Adieu’.
Composed in 1835.

69/2.about: A nostalgic, gently melancholy waltz in B minor, simpler and more youthful in style than Chopin’s later, more brilliant waltzes.
69/2.ctx: Composed in 1829, while Chopin was still in Warsaw, and published only after his death in 1855. It is among the earliest of his surviving waltzes.
facts: Composed in 1829, before Chopin left Poland.
Published posthumously in 1855.
One of the earliest waltzes Chopin is known to have written.

70/1.about: A lively, dancing waltz in G-flat major with a lyrical, more relaxed central trio section, its brightness and charm typical of Chopin’s Parisian salon style.
70/1.ctx: Composed around 1833 and published posthumously in 1855 as part of a set of three waltzes gathered by Julian Fontana from Chopin’s papers.
facts: The first of the three posthumous Op. 70 waltzes.
Published in 1855 by Julian Fontana.
Composed around 1833.

70/2.about: A melancholy, flowing waltz in F minor, its restrained sadness and gently undulating melody giving it a more introspective character than the brighter waltzes around it.
70/2.ctx: Composed around 1841 and, like its companions in Op. 70, published only after Chopin’s death by Fontana.
facts: The second of the three posthumous Op. 70 waltzes.
Composed around 1841.
More melancholy in character than most of Chopin’s waltzes.

70/3.about: A gentle waltz in D-flat major with an intimate, song-like melody, modest in scale and closer in spirit to a nocturne than to the more brilliant concert waltzes.
70/3.ctx: Composed around 1829, among Chopin’s earliest surviving waltzes, and published posthumously in 1855 as the last of the Op. 70 set.
facts: The last of the three posthumous Op. 70 waltzes.
Composed around 1829, during Chopin’s Warsaw years.
Its intimate melody resembles a nocturne more than a dance.

38.about: A ballade built on stark contrast: a gentle, pastoral song in F major, marked Andantino, alternates with sudden, violent storms in A minor, the two ideas colliding ever more forcefully until the piece is swept away in the final tempest.
38.ctx: The second of Chopin’s four ballades, begun in 1836 and completed during his stay in Majorca and at Nohant. Robert Schumann, to whom it is dedicated, noted that Chopin had played him a different, calmer ending when they met in 1836, before the more turbulent final version was published.
facts: Dedicated to Robert Schumann, who dedicated his Kreisleriana to Chopin in return.
Chopin reportedly played Schumann an earlier, gentler ending in 1836.
Alternates a pastoral melody with violent outbursts throughout.

47.about: A graceful, lilting ballade in A-flat major whose buoyant, dance-like narrative unfolds with less overt tragedy than its companions, moving through richly varied episodes to a bright, energetic close.
47.ctx: The third of the four ballades, composed in 1841 and dedicated to Mademoiselle Pauline de Noailles, one of Chopin’s pupils. Its warmth and comparative optimism set it apart from the darker First and Fourth Ballades.
facts: The third of Chopin’s four ballades.
Dedicated to his pupil Pauline de Noailles.
Generally considered the sunniest of the four ballades.

20.about: Violent, restless outer sections in B minor, full of driving dissonant chords, frame a hushed, tender middle section built on the Polish Christmas carol ‘Lulajże Jezuniu’ — an extraordinary contrast of ferocity and lullaby-like calm.
20.ctx: The first of Chopin’s four scherzos, begun around 1831, while news reached him in Vienna of the failed Polish uprising against Russia, and completed in Paris. Its stark violence has often been linked to Chopin’s grief and anger over Poland’s fate.
facts: Its central section quotes a Polish Christmas carol.
Its ferocity has often been linked to the failed 1830–31 Polish uprising.
Chopin’s first work to establish the scherzo as an independent, large-scale piano genre.

39.about: Fierce, driving octaves in C-sharp minor alternate with a chorale-like theme decorated by cascading falling arpeggios, the two ideas locked in dramatic opposition until a blazing, virtuosic close.
39.ctx: The third of the four scherzos, composed in 1839 and dedicated to Adolphe Gutmann, one of Chopin’s most devoted pupils. Its stark contrast between violent octaves and a hymn-like chorale gives it an almost combative structure.
facts: The third of Chopin’s four scherzos.
Dedicated to his pupil Adolphe Gutmann.
Built on the contrast between driving octaves and a chorale-like theme.

54.about: The lightest, most luminous of the four scherzos, its quicksilver E major textures dancing and darting with a wit and transparency unlike the darker drama of its predecessors.
54.ctx: The last of Chopin’s four scherzos, composed in 1842. Its sunnier disposition and lighter textures make it something of an outlier among the set, closer in spirit to a brilliant, high-spirited finale than to a tragic drama.
facts: The last and generally considered the sunniest of the four scherzos.
Composed in 1842, the same year as the Fourth Ballade.
Noted for its unusually light, transparent textures.

4.about: A youthful, ambitious sonata written as a conservatory exercise, its most unusual feature a slow movement cast in the rare metre of 5/4, an experimental touch unlike anything in Chopin’s later, more assured works.
4.ctx: Composed in 1828 while Chopin was still a student of Józef Elsner at the Warsaw Conservatory, to whom it is dedicated, and published only in 1851, two years after Chopin’s death. It is rarely performed today, overshadowed by his two later, more mature sonatas.
parts: A minuet that functions as a scherzo.
A slow movement in the unusual metre of five beats to the bar.
facts: Its slow movement is written in the unusual metre of 5/4.
Composed as a student exercise for Chopin’s teacher Józef Elsner.
Published posthumously, two years after Chopin’s death.

58.about: Chopin’s most expansive and classically proportioned sonata, opening with a broad, noble Allegro, followed by a light scherzo, a dreamy, songful Largo, and a heroic, sweeping finale in rondo form.
58.ctx: The third and last of Chopin’s piano sonatas, composed in 1844 and dedicated to Countess Émilie de Perthuis. It is regarded as the most successfully unified and large-scaled of his three sonatas.
facts: The last and most classically balanced of Chopin’s three piano sonatas.
Dedicated to Countess Émilie de Perthuis.
Composed in 1844, five years before Chopin’s death.

26/1.about: A proud yet lyrical polonaise in C-sharp minor, its noble dotted-rhythm main theme giving way to a tender, more songful middle section before the opening dignity returns.
26/1.ctx: The first of the two Op. 26 polonaises, composed around 1834–35 and dedicated to Joseph Dessauer. It marks Chopin’s return to the polonaise after several years, now reimagined as a large-scale concert work rather than a ceremonial dance.
facts: The first of the two Op. 26 polonaises.
Dedicated to the composer Joseph Dessauer.
Marks Chopin’s return to the polonaise as a concert genre.

26/2.about: A dark, menacing polonaise in E-flat minor, its ominous main theme and turbulent middle section giving it a brooding intensity that has earned it the unofficial nickname ‘Siberian’.
26/2.ctx: The second of the Op. 26 polonaises, composed alongside its companion around 1834–35. Its grim character is sometimes linked, though without firm evidence, to the fate of Polish exiles sent to Siberia after the failed 1830 uprising.
facts: Sometimes nicknamed the ‘Siberian’ polonaise.
The second of the two Op. 26 polonaises.
One of the darkest and most turbulent of all Chopin’s polonaises.

40/1.about: A bold, festive polonaise in A major, built on ringing, confident chords and a triumphant martial spirit that has made it, alongside the ‘Heroic’, one of Chopin’s most popular polonaises; it carries the nickname ‘Military’.
40/1.ctx: The first of the two Op. 40 polonaises, composed in 1838 and dedicated to Julian Fontana. Its bright, patriotic energy made it an instant favourite and remains one of the most frequently performed of all Chopin’s works.
facts: Nicknamed the ‘Military’ polonaise.
Dedicated to Julian Fontana, Chopin’s friend and copyist.
One of Chopin’s most popular and frequently performed pieces.

40/2.about: A sombre, brooding polonaise in C minor, its melody carried in the left hand beneath a darker, more anxious texture than the confident brightness of its companion piece.
40/2.ctx: The second of the Op. 40 polonaises, composed around 1838–39, during the difficult winter Chopin spent in Majorca. Its grim, weighted character stands in deliberate contrast to the ‘Military’ Polonaise that precedes it.
facts: The second of the two Op. 40 polonaises.
Its main melody is carried in the left hand.
Composed around the time of Chopin’s difficult stay in Majorca.

44.about: A grand, dramatic polonaise in F-sharp minor of unusual scale and ambition, its stormy outer sections interrupted by an unexpected mazurka set into the middle of the work, a striking formal experiment.
44.ctx: Composed in 1840–41 and dedicated to Princess Anna Czartoryska. Its scope and the insertion of an entire mazurka within its structure make it one of the most formally daring of all Chopin’s polonaises.
facts: Contains an entire mazurka embedded within its middle section.
Dedicated to Princess Anna Czartoryska.
One of the longest and most structurally ambitious of Chopin’s polonaises.

61.about: A free, improvisatory late masterpiece that blends the polonaise with the fantasy, its continuously evolving material never settling into a straightforward statement of the dance rhythm until deep into the piece.
61.ctx: Composed in 1845–46 and dedicated to Madame A. Veyret. Known as the ‘Polonaise-Fantaisie’, it represents the furthest extension of the genre, more a continuous musical narrative than a dance-based concert piece.
facts: Known as the ‘Polonaise-Fantaisie’ for its free, evolving form.
The last of Chopin’s major polonaises.
Dedicated to Madame A. Veyret.

posth-pol.about: Chopin’s first published composition, written at the age of seven: a brief, charming polonaise in G minor, modest in scale but already showing an unmistakable feel for the dance rhythm that would define so much of his later output.
posth-pol.ctx: Published in Warsaw in 1817 with the help of Chopin’s teacher and family friends, who recognised the boy’s precocious gift; it appeared in print before Chopin had turned eight years old, making him a minor celebrity in Warsaw society.
facts: Chopin’s earliest published work, written at age seven.
Published in Warsaw when Chopin was not yet eight.
Already unmistakably built on the polonaise rhythm.

6/1.about: An early mazurka in F-sharp minor, melancholy and ornately decorated, its rubato-laden melody already showing the freedom Chopin brought to the Polish dance.
6/1.ctx: One of the four mazurkas of Op. 6, composed in 1830 and dedicated to the Countess Pauline Plater, among the first mazurkas Chopin published and the works with which he introduced the genre to Paris.
facts: The first of the four Op. 6 mazurkas.
Among the first mazurkas Chopin published.
Dedicated to the Countess Pauline Plater.

6/2.about: A mazurka in C-sharp minor that opens with a drone-like introduction evoking the sound of a village bagpipe, before a livelier folk-inflected dance begins.
6/2.ctx: One of the four mazurkas of Op. 6, composed in 1830 and dedicated to the Countess Pauline Plater, among the first mazurkas Chopin published and the works with which he introduced the genre to Paris.
facts: Opens with a bagpipe-like drone.
The second of the four Op. 6 mazurkas.
Composed in 1830.

6/3.about: A lively, rustic mazurka in E major with strong accents on the weak beats, capturing the vigorous foot-stamping character of the Polish folk dance.
6/3.ctx: One of the four mazurkas of Op. 6, composed in 1830 and dedicated to the Countess Pauline Plater, among the first mazurkas Chopin published and the works with which he introduced the genre to Paris.
facts: The third of the four Op. 6 mazurkas.
Marked by strong, folk-dance accents.
Part of Chopin’s first published set of mazurkas.

6/4.about: A tiny, circling miniature in E-flat minor, its brief, repetitive melody giving it an almost hypnotic, incomplete quality.
6/4.ctx: One of the four mazurkas of Op. 6, composed in 1830 and dedicated to the Countess Pauline Plater, among the first mazurkas Chopin published and the works with which he introduced the genre to Paris.
facts: The shortest of the four Op. 6 mazurkas.
Its melody circles repetitively within a narrow range.
Composed in 1830, before Chopin settled in Paris.

7/1.about: A buoyant, immediately popular mazurka in B-flat major with a rustic, drone-like trio section, one of the best-known of all Chopin’s mazurkas.
7/1.ctx: One of the five mazurkas of Op. 7, composed around 1830–32 and dedicated to Paul Émile Johns, published alongside Op. 6 as Chopin’s introduction of the mazurka to Parisian audiences.
facts: One of the most popular of all Chopin’s mazurkas.
The first of the five Op. 7 mazurkas.
Its trio imitates a rustic drone.

7/2.about: A melancholy dance in A minor whose plaintive main theme is set against a brighter, more animated central episode.
7/2.ctx: One of the five mazurkas of Op. 7, composed around 1830–32 and dedicated to Paul Émile Johns, published alongside Op. 6 as Chopin’s introduction of the mazurka to Parisian audiences.
facts: The second of the five Op. 7 mazurkas.
Alternates melancholy and brighter episodes.
Composed around 1830–31.

7/3.about: An energetic mazurka in F minor built on strong, insistent accents, its dance rhythm driven forward with unusual force.
7/3.ctx: One of the five mazurkas of Op. 7, composed around 1830–32 and dedicated to Paul Émile Johns, published alongside Op. 6 as Chopin’s introduction of the mazurka to Parisian audiences.
facts: The third of the five Op. 7 mazurkas.
Notable for its forceful, insistent accents.
Part of Chopin’s early set of published mazurkas.

7/4.about: A short, lively mazurka in A-flat major, its quick tempo and modest scale making it one of the more fleeting pieces of the set.
7/4.ctx: One of the five mazurkas of Op. 7, composed around 1830–32 and dedicated to Paul Émile Johns, published alongside Op. 6 as Chopin’s introduction of the mazurka to Parisian audiences.
facts: The fourth of the five Op. 7 mazurkas.
One of the briefest mazurkas Chopin wrote.
Composed around 1830–31.

7/5.about: A tiny mazurka in C major marked to be repeated ‘without end’, its brief melody looping back on itself rather than closing conventionally.
7/5.ctx: One of the five mazurkas of Op. 7, composed around 1830–32 and dedicated to Paul Émile Johns, published alongside Op. 6 as Chopin’s introduction of the mazurka to Parisian audiences.
facts: Marked to repeat ‘senza fine’ — without end.
The last of the five Op. 7 mazurkas.
One of Chopin’s shortest and most enigmatic mazurkas.

17/1.about: A bright, confident mazurka in B-flat major with a strongly accented, dance-forward rhythm typical of the vivace mazurka type.
17/1.ctx: One of the four mazurkas of Op. 17, composed in 1832–33 in Paris and dedicated to Lina Freppa, an Italian singer active in Parisian salon society.
facts: The first of the four Op. 17 mazurkas.
Dedicated to the singer Lina Freppa.
Composed in Chopin’s early Paris years.

17/2.about: A wistful, lilting mazurka in E minor, its gently swaying melody carrying a note of tender melancholy.
17/2.ctx: One of the four mazurkas of Op. 17, composed in 1832–33 in Paris and dedicated to Lina Freppa, an Italian singer active in Parisian salon society.
facts: The second of the four Op. 17 mazurkas.
Composed in 1832–33.
Notable for its wistful, songlike lilt.

17/3.about: A gentle mazurka in A-flat major whose middle section wanders through unexpected, chromatic harmony before the simpler opening returns.
17/3.ctx: One of the four mazurkas of Op. 17, composed in 1832–33 in Paris and dedicated to Lina Freppa, an Italian singer active in Parisian salon society.
facts: The third of the four Op. 17 mazurkas.
Its middle section is notably chromatic.
Part of Chopin’s early Paris output.

17/4.about: A haunting mazurka in A minor that begins and ends on an unresolved harmony, giving the whole piece a fragile, suspended, unfinished quality.
17/4.ctx: One of the four mazurkas of Op. 17, composed in 1832–33 in Paris and dedicated to Lina Freppa, an Italian singer active in Parisian salon society.
facts: Begins and ends without harmonic resolution.
The last and most harmonically unusual of the Op. 17 mazurkas.
Often considered the most emotionally ambiguous of Chopin’s early mazurkas.

24/1.about: A plaintive, lilting mazurka in G minor, its simple melody carrying a restrained, understated sadness.
24/1.ctx: One of the four mazurkas of Op. 24, composed in 1834–35 and dedicated to the Comte de Perthuis, an aide-de-camp to King Louis-Philippe.
facts: The first of the four Op. 24 mazurkas.
Dedicated to the Comte de Perthuis.
Composed in 1834–35.

24/2.about: A bright mazurka in C major with modal, folk-like inflections that give it an archaic, rustic flavour unusual even among Chopin’s mazurkas.
24/2.ctx: One of the four mazurkas of Op. 24, composed in 1834–35 and dedicated to the Comte de Perthuis, an aide-de-camp to King Louis-Philippe.
facts: Notable for its modal, folk-like harmony.
The second of the four Op. 24 mazurkas.
One of the more overtly rustic mazurkas in Chopin’s output.

24/3.about: A short, graceful mazurka in A-flat major, modest in scale and gentle in character, offering a moment of repose within the set.
24/3.ctx: One of the four mazurkas of Op. 24, composed in 1834–35 and dedicated to the Comte de Perthuis, an aide-de-camp to King Louis-Philippe.
facts: The third of the four Op. 24 mazurkas.
One of the briefer, gentler pieces in the set.
Composed alongside its companions in 1834–35.

24/4.about: An extended mazurka of rich harmonic contrasts in B-flat minor, its wide range of moods closing in a hushed, gradually fading coda.
24/4.ctx: One of the four mazurkas of Op. 24, composed in 1834–35 and dedicated to the Comte de Perthuis, an aide-de-camp to King Louis-Philippe.
facts: The longest and most developed of the Op. 24 mazurkas.
Ends in a quiet, fading coda.
Closes the Op. 24 set.

30/1.about: A brief, melancholy mazurka in C minor, its subdued mood and modest scale setting a quiet tone for the set.
30/1.ctx: One of the four mazurkas of Op. 30, composed in 1836–37 and dedicated to Princess Maria de Württemberg, a former pupil of Chopin.
facts: The first of the four Op. 30 mazurkas.
Dedicated to Princess Maria de Württemberg.
Composed in 1836–37.

30/2.about: A lively, folk-like mazurka in B minor, its quick tempo and rustic accents giving it an energetic, dance-forward character.
30/2.ctx: One of the four mazurkas of Op. 30, composed in 1836–37 and dedicated to Princess Maria de Württemberg, a former pupil of Chopin.
facts: The second of the four Op. 30 mazurkas.
Notable for its lively, folk-dance energy.
Part of the Op. 30 set dedicated to Princess Württemberg.

30/3.about: A proud mazurka in D-flat major built on striking major–minor echo effects, its harmonic ambiguity lending it a wry, unsettled character beneath its confident surface.
30/3.ctx: One of the four mazurkas of Op. 30, composed in 1836–37 and dedicated to Princess Maria de Württemberg, a former pupil of Chopin.
facts: Notable for its major–minor echo effects.
The third of the four Op. 30 mazurkas.
Composed in 1836–37.

30/4.about: A dark, dramatic mazurka in C-sharp minor with striking parallel harmonies and an unusually intense, chromatic close, considered one of the finest of the whole set.
30/4.ctx: One of the four mazurkas of Op. 30, composed in 1836–37 and dedicated to Princess Maria de Württemberg, a former pupil of Chopin.
facts: Widely regarded as the finest of the Op. 30 mazurkas.
Closes the set with unusual chromatic intensity.
Composed in 1836–37.

33/1.about: A brief, sorrowful mazurka in G-sharp minor, its restrained melancholy setting a subdued tone for the opus.
33/1.ctx: One of the four mazurkas of Op. 33, composed in 1837–38 and dedicated to the Countess Rosa Mostowska.
facts: The first of the four Op. 33 mazurkas.
Dedicated to the Countess Rosa Mostowska.
Composed in 1837–38.
