33/2.about: An exuberant dance in D major built on swirling, repeated figures, its energy and popularity making it one of the best-known mazurkas of the set.
33/2.ctx: One of the four mazurkas of Op. 33, composed in 1837–38 and dedicated to the Countess Rosa Mostowska.
facts: One of the more popular and frequently performed of Chopin’s mazurkas.
The second of the four Op. 33 mazurkas.
Notable for its swirling, repetitive figuration.

33/3.about: A simple, gentle mazurka in C major, unpretentious and modest in scale, offering understated charm rather than overt drama.
33/3.ctx: One of the four mazurkas of Op. 33, composed in 1837–38 and dedicated to the Countess Rosa Mostowska.
facts: The third of the four Op. 33 mazurkas.
One of the simplest and most understated mazurkas Chopin wrote.
Composed in 1837–38.

33/4.about: An extended, ballad-like mazurka in B minor, its unusually long span and evolving material giving it a narrative quality closer to the ballades than to the shorter mazurkas.
33/4.ctx: One of the four mazurkas of Op. 33, composed in 1837–38 and dedicated to the Countess Rosa Mostowska.
facts: The longest and most extended of the Op. 33 mazurkas.
Its scale has led some to compare it to Chopin’s ballades.
Closes the Op. 33 set.

41/1.about: A plaintive mazurka in E minor whose subdued, searching melody carries an unusually restrained, introspective sadness.
41/1.ctx: One of the four mazurkas of Op. 41, composed between 1838 and 1839 and dedicated to the poet Stefan Witwicki, a close friend of Chopin whose verses he also set as songs. Their numbering within the opus varies between different editions.
facts: Part of the four Op. 41 mazurkas, dedicated to the poet Stefan Witwicki.
Composed during Chopin’s difficult winter in Majorca.
Its numbering has varied between different editions.

41/2.about: A graceful, flowing mazurka in B major, its warm major-key lyricism offering contrast to the more troubled mazurkas around it.
41/2.ctx: One of the four mazurkas of Op. 41, composed between 1838 and 1839 and dedicated to the poet Stefan Witwicki, a close friend of Chopin whose verses he also set as songs. Their numbering within the opus varies between different editions.
facts: One of the more lyrical mazurkas in Op. 41.
Composed around 1838–39.
Dedicated, with the set, to Stefan Witwicki.

41/3.about: A lively, spirited mazurka in A-flat major, its quick tempo and dance energy contrasting with the more introspective pieces of the set.
41/3.ctx: One of the four mazurkas of Op. 41, composed between 1838 and 1839 and dedicated to the poet Stefan Witwicki, a close friend of Chopin whose verses he also set as songs. Their numbering within the opus varies between different editions.
facts: Among the livelier mazurkas of Op. 41.
Composed during Chopin’s stay in Majorca and at Nohant.
Part of the set dedicated to Stefan Witwicki.

41/4.about: An introspective mazurka in C-sharp minor with a modal, archaic-sounding opening, its harmony lending it an unusually old, folk-rooted character.
41/4.ctx: One of the four mazurkas of Op. 41, composed between 1838 and 1839 and dedicated to the poet Stefan Witwicki, a close friend of Chopin whose verses he also set as songs. Their numbering within the opus varies between different editions.
facts: Notable for its modal, archaic harmony.
The last of the four Op. 41 mazurkas.
Composed during a difficult period of Chopin’s life.

50/1.about: A cheerful, sunny mazurka in G major, its bright, uncomplicated melody among the more good-humoured of Chopin’s later mazurkas.
50/1.ctx: One of the three mazurkas of Op. 50, composed in 1841–42 and dedicated to Leon Szmitkowski.
facts: The first of the three Op. 50 mazurkas.
Dedicated to Leon Szmitkowski.
Composed in 1841–42.

50/2.about: A graceful, lilting mazurka in A-flat major, its flowing melody and gentle rhythm typical of Chopin’s mature mazurka style.
50/2.ctx: One of the three mazurkas of Op. 50, composed in 1841–42 and dedicated to Leon Szmitkowski.
facts: The second of the three Op. 50 mazurkas.
Composed alongside its companions in 1841–42.
Part of the set dedicated to Leon Szmitkowski.

50/3.about: A contrapuntal, expansive mazurka in C-sharp minor of unusual depth, weaving fugal textures into the dance form in a display of Chopin’s late absorption of Bach’s counterpoint.
50/3.ctx: One of the three mazurkas of Op. 50, composed in 1841–42 and dedicated to Leon Szmitkowski.
facts: Notable for its fugal, contrapuntal writing.
Considered one of the most sophisticated mazurkas Chopin wrote.
Closes the Op. 50 set.

56/1.about: An expansive, harmonically restless mazurka in B major, its wandering tonality and extended form pushing at the boundaries of the genre.
56/1.ctx: One of the three mazurkas of Op. 56, composed in 1843 and dedicated to Catherine Maberly, an English pupil of Chopin.
facts: The first of the three Op. 56 mazurkas.
Dedicated to Chopin’s English pupil Catherine Maberly.
Notable for its restless, wandering harmony.

56/2.about: A rustic dance in C major built over sustained drone fifths, evoking the sound of Polish folk instruments more directly than most of Chopin’s later mazurkas.
56/2.ctx: One of the three mazurkas of Op. 56, composed in 1843 and dedicated to Catherine Maberly, an English pupil of Chopin.
facts: Built over sustained drone fifths, evoking folk instruments.
The second of the three Op. 56 mazurkas.
Composed in 1843.

56/3.about: A long, complex mazurka in C minor of considerable depth, its continuously evolving material and unusual length making it one of the most ambitious of all Chopin’s mazurkas.
56/3.ctx: One of the three mazurkas of Op. 56, composed in 1843 and dedicated to Catherine Maberly, an English pupil of Chopin.
facts: One of the longest and most structurally complex mazurkas Chopin wrote.
Closes the Op. 56 set.
Composed in 1843.

59/1.about: A melancholy, chromatically rich mazurka in A minor, its harmony shifting restlessly beneath a plaintive melody.
59/1.ctx: One of the three mazurkas of Op. 59, composed in 1845 and, unusually, published without a personal dedication.
facts: The first of the three Op. 59 mazurkas.
Composed in 1845, published without a dedication.
Notable for its rich chromatic harmony.

59/2.about: A graceful, warm mazurka in A-flat major, its flowing lines and gentle harmony among the more consoling of Chopin’s late mazurkas.
59/2.ctx: One of the three mazurkas of Op. 59, composed in 1845 and, unusually, published without a personal dedication.
facts: The second of the three Op. 59 mazurkas.
Considered one of the warmer, more lyrical late mazurkas.
Composed in 1845.

59/3.about: An energetic, proud mazurka in F-sharp minor that closes with a brilliant coda, ending the set with considerable virtuosic flourish.
59/3.ctx: One of the three mazurkas of Op. 59, composed in 1845 and, unusually, published without a personal dedication.
facts: Ends the Op. 59 set with a brilliant coda.
The third of the three Op. 59 mazurkas.
Composed in 1845.

63/1.about: A lively late mazurka in B major, its confident, dance-forward energy showing little sign of the declining health Chopin suffered in his final years.
63/1.ctx: One of the three mazurkas of Op. 63, composed in 1846 and dedicated to the Countess Laura Czosnowska.
facts: The first of the three Op. 63 mazurkas.
Dedicated to the Countess Laura Czosnowska.
Composed in 1846, three years before Chopin’s death.

63/2.about: A brief, melancholy late mazurka in F minor, its subdued, understated sadness typical of Chopin’s final mazurkas.
63/2.ctx: One of the three mazurkas of Op. 63, composed in 1846 and dedicated to the Countess Laura Czosnowska.
facts: The second of the three Op. 63 mazurkas.
Composed in 1846.
One of the more subdued of Chopin’s late mazurkas.

63/3.about: A graceful late mazurka in C-sharp minor that closes with a brief canon between the hands, a subtle contrapuntal touch typical of Chopin’s final years.
63/3.ctx: One of the three mazurkas of Op. 63, composed in 1846 and dedicated to the Countess Laura Czosnowska.
facts: Closes with a short canon between the hands.
The last of the three Op. 63 mazurkas.
One of the last mazurkas Chopin published in his lifetime.

67/1.about: A bright mazurka in G major, cheerful and dance-like, published only after Chopin’s death.
67/1.ctx: Composed around 1835 but withheld from publication during Chopin’s lifetime; it was issued in 1855 as part of a posthumous collection of mazurkas assembled by Julian Fontana from Chopin’s manuscripts.
facts: Published posthumously in 1855 by Julian Fontana.
Composed around 1835.
One of four mazurkas gathered as Op. 67 after Chopin’s death.

67/2.about: A wistful mazurka in G minor, one of the last Chopin composed, its subdued melancholy reflecting his declining health in his final year.
67/2.ctx: Composed in 1848 or 1849, among the very last pieces Chopin wrote, during the year of his final illness and death; published posthumously by Fontana in 1855.
facts: Among the last pieces Chopin composed.
Written during his final year of failing health.
Published posthumously in 1855.

67/3.about: A simple, gentle mazurka in C major, modest and unassuming, one of several early mazurkas Chopin chose not to publish during his lifetime.
67/3.ctx: Composed around 1835 and, like its companions in Op. 67, withheld from publication until it appeared posthumously in Fontana’s 1855 edition.
facts: Composed around 1835.
Withheld from publication during Chopin’s lifetime.
Published posthumously as part of Op. 67.

67/4.about: A melancholy, lyrical mazurka in A minor, its flowing sadness typical of Chopin’s later mazurka style.
67/4.ctx: Composed around 1846 and published posthumously in 1855, closing the set of four mazurkas gathered by Fontana as Op. 67.
facts: Closes the posthumous Op. 67 set.
Composed around 1846.
Published six years after Chopin’s death.

68/1.about: A youthful, lively mazurka in C major, composed while Chopin was still a student, published only after his death.
68/1.ctx: Composed in 1829 in Warsaw and published posthumously in 1855 as the first of four mazurkas gathered by Julian Fontana, spanning the earliest and latest years of Chopin’s life.
facts: Composed in 1829, during Chopin’s student years in Warsaw.
The first of the posthumous Op. 68 mazurkas.
Published in 1855, six years after his death.

68/2.about: A melancholy, lyrical mazurka in A minor, among the very earliest surviving pieces Chopin composed, written when he was around seventeen.
68/2.ctx: Composed around 1827, when Chopin was still a teenager, making it one of his earliest surviving mazurkas; it was published only in 1855, as part of the posthumous Op. 68 collection.
facts: One of the earliest mazurkas Chopin is known to have composed.
Written when Chopin was around seventeen.
Published posthumously in 1855.

68/3.about: A rustic mazurka in F major with a bagpipe-like drone in its trio section, youthful and folk-inflected in character.
68/3.ctx: Composed around 1830, shortly before Chopin left Poland permanently, and published posthumously in 1855 as part of the Op. 68 set.
facts: Composed around 1830, shortly before Chopin left Poland.
Its trio imitates a rustic bagpipe drone.
Part of the posthumous Op. 68 collection.

68/4.about: Traditionally regarded as Chopin’s last composition: a fragile, chromatic sketch in F minor, left unfinished at his death and later completed for publication by other hands.
68/4.ctx: Composed in 1849, the year of Chopin’s death, and left incomplete; the version usually performed was reconstructed from his sketches for the 1855 posthumous edition. Its halting, unresolved character has long been read as a poignant farewell.
facts: Traditionally considered Chopin’s last composition.
Left unfinished at his death and completed by later editors.
Published posthumously in 1855.

29.about: Flowing, whirling triplets in A-flat major run continuously around a more lyrical, songful middle section in F minor, the piece returning to its rippling opening for a bright close.
29.ctx: The first of Chopin’s three numbered impromptus, composed in 1837 and dedicated to Mademoiselle Caroline de Lobau. It established the free, rhapsodic character that would define the genre for him.
facts: The first of Chopin’s three numbered impromptus.
Dedicated to Mademoiselle Caroline de Lobau.
Composed in 1837.

36.about: An unusual impromptu that opens like a nocturne, with a gently rocking barcarolle-like melody, before an unexpected, march-like episode intrudes and the piece works its way back to a transformed close.
36.ctx: The second of Chopin’s three impromptus, composed in 1839. Its unpredictable, almost improvisatory structure — nocturne giving way to march — makes it the most formally adventurous of the set.
facts: The second of Chopin’s three impromptus.
Combines a nocturne-like opening with an unexpected march episode.
Composed in 1839.

51.about: A gentle, flowing impromptu in G-flat major whose warm main theme is interrupted by a darker, more searching middle section before the opening lyricism returns.
51.ctx: The third and last of Chopin’s numbered impromptus, composed in 1842. It is less frequently performed than its companions, but shares their improvisatory freedom and lyrical warmth.
facts: The last of Chopin’s three numbered impromptus.
Composed in 1842, the same year as the Fourth Ballade.
Less often performed than his first two impromptus.

60.about: A Venetian gondola song transformed into one of Chopin’s richest and most harmonically sophisticated late works, its rocking 12/8 barcarolle rhythm supporting an increasingly ornate and passionate melody that builds to a grand, resonant climax.
60.ctx: Composed in 1845–46 and dedicated to Baroness de Stockhausen, the Barcarolle represents the summit of Chopin’s late style, its lush harmony and structural ambition placing it among his most admired works by pianists and composers alike.
facts: Regarded by many pianists as one of Chopin’s greatest works.
Dedicated to the Baroness de Stockhausen.
Transforms the simple Venetian boat-song into an extended, richly developed piece.

57.about: A lullaby built on a gently rocking, unchanging bass figure in D-flat major, above which an increasingly elaborate stream of variations unfolds, the melody dissolving into ever more delicate figuration without ever disturbing the calm.
57.ctx: Composed in 1843–44 and dedicated to Elise Gavard, one of Chopin’s pupils. Its combination of harmonic stillness in the bass with soaring decorative freedom above makes it one of his most original formal inventions.
facts: Built over an unchanging, gently rocking bass throughout.
Dedicated to Chopin’s pupil Elise Gavard.
One of Chopin’s most formally original works.

49.about: A march-like opening leads into a sequence of impassioned, dramatically contrasted episodes, before the piece settles into a hushed, chorale-like passage and closes with a return of impassioned energy — a large-scale, freely narrative structure unlike any other Chopin work.
49.ctx: Composed in 1841 and dedicated to Princess Catherine de Souzzo. Its ambitious scale and free, evolving form place it alongside the ballades as one of Chopin’s most substantial single-movement works.
facts: Dedicated to Princess Catherine de Souzzo.
One of the largest and most ambitious of all Chopin’s single-movement works.
Composed in 1841.

43.about: A breathless Italian dance in perpetual motion, its rapid 6/8 figuration and unflagging energy in A-flat major making it one of the most purely virtuosic of Chopin’s shorter concert pieces.
43.ctx: Composed in 1841, the Tarantelle is Chopin’s single essay in the whirlwind Neapolitan dance form associated with the bite of the tarantula spider, a genre also taken up by Liszt and other virtuoso composers of the era.
facts: Chopin’s only work in the tarantella genre.
Composed in 1841.
Modelled on the whirling Italian dance associated with the tarantula.

19.about: A bright, Spanish-tinged concert piece in C major that opens with a march-like introduction before settling into a polonaise-like dance rhythm, its exotic dance flavour and bolero name unusual within Chopin’s output.
19.ctx: Composed in 1833 and dedicated to Countess Emilia Elzanowska. Chopin originally titled the piece ‘Souvenir d’Andalousie’ before settling on ‘Bolero’, reflecting the vogue for Spanish colour in Parisian salons of the period.
facts: Chopin originally titled it ‘Souvenir d’Andalousie’.
His only work to carry the name ‘Bolero’.
Combines Spanish dance rhythm with the accent of a Polish polonaise.

22.about: A calm, nocturne-like Andante spianato in G major, added later as a serene introduction, leads without pause into the dazzling Grande Polonaise brillante, a brilliant concert showpiece of glittering figuration and orchestral grandeur.
22.ctx: The Grande Polonaise was composed in 1830–31 for piano and orchestra, before Chopin left Poland; the Andante spianato, an independent piece for solo piano, was added in 1834 to serve as its introduction. The combined work is dedicated to Baroness d’Est.
parts: A calm, smoothly flowing introduction for solo piano, added in 1834.
A brilliant polonaise for piano and orchestra, composed in 1830–31.
facts: The Andante spianato was added four years after the Grande Polonaise.
Originally conceived for piano and orchestra.
Dedicated to Baroness d’Est.

11.about: A lyrical, large-scale concerto whose outer movements frame a dreamy, nocturne-like Romanze and close with a spirited finale built on the rhythm of the krakowiak, a lively Polish folk dance.
11.ctx: Composed in 1830, shortly before Chopin left Poland forever, and dedicated to Friedrich Kalkbrenner, the celebrated pianist whose playing Chopin greatly admired. Despite being numbered first, it was actually composed after the Concerto in F minor.
parts: A broad orchestral opening leading to the piano’s lyrical entrance.
A spirited finale built on the krakowiak dance rhythm.
facts: Dedicated to the pianist Friedrich Kalkbrenner.
Numbered first but actually composed after the F minor Concerto.
Its finale is built on the krakowiak, a Polish folk dance.

21.about: Chopin’s earlier piano concerto, though published second, prized above all for its heartfelt central Larghetto, said to have been inspired by his youthful infatuation with the singer Konstancja Gładkowska; the finale closes with a mazurka-inflected rondo.
21.ctx: Composed in 1829, before the concerto later numbered first, and dedicated to Countess Delfina Potocka. Chopin himself wrote that the slow movement was inspired by feelings for ‘a young person’ he loved but had not yet told.
parts: A broad orchestral opening leading to the soloist’s entrance.
A tender slow movement said to have been inspired by Konstancja Gładkowska.
A lively finale built on a mazurka rhythm.
facts: Actually composed before the concerto numbered first.
Its Larghetto is said to reflect Chopin’s feelings for the singer Konstancja Gładkowska.
Dedicated to Countess Delfina Potocka.

65.about: Chopin’s only mature chamber work, a substantial four-movement sonata in G minor for cello and piano that treats both instruments as equal partners, its intricate piano writing and searching harmony marking a departure from the brilliance of his concert works.
65.ctx: Composed in 1845–46 for the cellist Auguste Franchomme, a close friend, and dedicated to him; it was the last work Chopin completed and one of very few he wrote for an instrument other than solo piano.
parts: A substantial opening movement with equal weight given to both instruments.
A restless scherzo with a lyrical trio.
facts: The last work Chopin completed.
Dedicated to his close friend, the cellist Auguste Franchomme.
One of very few Chopin works for an instrument other than solo piano.

3.about: A brilliant salon piece for cello and piano, its brief slow introduction leading into a glittering, virtuosic polonaise, composed to be played with a skilled amateur cellist rather than as a serious chamber statement.
3.ctx: Composed in 1829–30 for Prince Antoni Radziwiłł, an amateur cellist and patron who had befriended the young Chopin, and with whose daughter Wanda Chopin is said to have been infatuated. It is dedicated to Prince Radziwiłł.
facts: Written for the amateur cellist Prince Antoni Radziwiłł.
Chopin is said to have been infatuated with the prince’s daughter Wanda.
A brilliant salon piece rather than a serious chamber statement.

14.about: A brilliant concert rondo for piano and orchestra built on the krakowiak, a lively Polish dance in syncopated duple time, its glittering piano writing framed by colourful orchestral accompaniment.
14.ctx: Composed in 1828, before Chopin left Poland, and dedicated to Princess Anna Czartoryska. It was one of the works with which the young Chopin sought to establish himself as a touring virtuoso in Vienna and beyond.
facts: Dedicated to Princess Anna Czartoryska.
Built on the krakowiak, a syncopated Polish folk dance.
Composed in 1828, before Chopin left Poland.

13.about: A large-scale fantasy for piano and orchestra built from a sequence of well-known Polish folk and patriotic melodies, moving from a slow, songful opening through a set of variations to a brilliant, dance-driven close.
13.ctx: Composed in 1828 and dedicated to Johann Peter Pixis, a pianist and composer Chopin knew in Paris. Its overtly nationalist material reflects the young composer’s pride in Polish folk culture before his permanent departure from Poland.
facts: Built on a sequence of well-known Polish folk and patriotic tunes.
Dedicated to the pianist and composer Johann Peter Pixis.
Composed in 1828, before Chopin left Poland for good.

46.about: A brilliant, large-scale concert work for solo piano, expansive and orchestral in conception, believed by some scholars to have begun life as the opening movement of a planned but abandoned third piano concerto.
46.ctx: Composed in 1840–41 and dedicated to Friederike Müller, one of Chopin’s most talented pupils. Its grand scale and orchestral textures, unusual for a solo piano piece, support the theory that it originated as concerto material.
facts: Possibly conceived as the first movement of an abandoned third piano concerto.
Dedicated to Chopin’s pupil Friederike Müller.
Composed in 1840–41.

2.about: A set of brilliant variations for piano and orchestra on ‘Là ci darem la mano’, the seductive duet from Mozart’s Don Giovanni, moving through increasingly virtuosic transformations of the tune to a dazzling polonaise-finale.
2.ctx: Composed in 1827 when Chopin was seventeen and dedicated to Tytus Woyciechowski, his closest friend. After hearing it in 1831, the young Robert Schumann famously wrote in a review, ‘Hats off, gentlemen — a genius!’, launching Chopin’s reputation in Germany.
parts: Five increasingly virtuosic variations followed by a brilliant polonaise finale.
facts: Schumann’s famous review — ‘Hats off, gentlemen, a genius!’ — launched Chopin’s German reputation.
Dedicated to Chopin’s closest friend, Tytus Woyciechowski.
Composed when Chopin was just seventeen.

1.about: Chopin’s official Op. 1: a youthful, brilliant rondo in C minor written as a teenager, its confident virtuosity and clear formal design showing the precocious technical assurance of the fifteen-year-old composer.
1.ctx: Composed in 1825 and dedicated to Countess Ludwika Linde, wife of the director of the Warsaw Lyceum that Chopin attended. It was the first work Chopin himself chose to designate with an opus number.
facts: The first work Chopin gave an opus number.
Composed when he was fifteen.
Dedicated to Countess Ludwika Linde.

5.about: An early rondo built on the rhythms of the mazurka, its bright, dance-driven main theme alternating with more lyrical episodes in a form that already anticipates Chopin’s lifelong fascination with the Polish dance.
5.ctx: Composed in 1826, while Chopin was still a student, and dedicated to Alexandrine de Moriolles, the daughter of a French tutor at the Warsaw court. It is among the earliest works in which Chopin fused a Western classical form with Polish folk rhythm.
facts: One of Chopin’s earliest fusions of Polish dance rhythm with a Western classical form.
Dedicated to Alexandrine de Moriolles.
Composed in 1826.

16.about: A brilliant, virtuoso rondo opening with a dramatic slow introduction before launching into a glittering, fast main section full of scales, leaps and rapid passagework in the showpiece manner of early-Romantic Paris.
16.ctx: Composed in 1832, shortly after Chopin’s arrival in Paris, and dedicated to Caroline Hartmann, one of his early pupils. It reflects the brilliant, crowd-pleasing style Chopin cultivated to establish himself in the competitive Parisian concert world.
facts: Composed shortly after Chopin settled in Paris.
Dedicated to his pupil Caroline Hartmann.
Opens with a dramatic slow introduction.

12.about: Brilliant variations on a popular air, ‘Je vends des scapulaires’, from Ferdinand Hérold’s opera Ludovic, moving through a sequence of increasingly virtuosic transformations in the fashionable operatic-variation style of the day.
12.ctx: Composed in 1833 for the Parisian publisher Maurice Schlesinger and dedicated to Émile Gaillard. It belongs to a genre of opera-tune variations that was hugely popular in Paris in the 1830s, a style Chopin otherwise mostly abandoned after his early years.
facts: Based on a tune from Hérold’s opera Ludovic.
Dedicated to Émile Gaillard.
One of Chopin’s few excursions into the fashionable genre of operatic variations.

posth-wish.about: A cheerful strophic song setting a poem by Stefan Witwicki, its simple, folk-like melody later transcribed for solo piano by Franz Liszt as part of his collection of Chopin song transcriptions.
posth-wish.ctx: Composed around 1829 as one of Chopin’s Polish songs, later gathered posthumously as Op. 74; Liszt’s piano transcription, published in 1860, helped bring the song to a wider instrumental audience after Chopin’s death.
posth-wish.sc: Voice and piano (also transcribed for solo piano by Liszt)
facts: Originally a song setting a poem by Stefan Witwicki.
Transcribed for solo piano by Franz Liszt.
Part of the posthumous collection of songs published as Op. 74.
